abstract: Economic Brief 26-26 from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, by Katarina Borovickova and Claudia Macaluso, published 2026-08-12. It decomposes the post-2023 decline in US job-finding rates by CPS reason-for-unemployment category and by occupational AI exposure, and reaches a conclusion that cuts against the dominant framing in this corpus: new entrants are not where the action is. Their job-finding decline is modest next to job losers and job leavers, and the authors set entrants aside entirely. The decline concentrates instead among strongly attached incumbent workers in highly AI-exposed occupations - roughly 13 percentage points against about 2 points for marginally attached workers. If that holds, a body of evidence currently read as an early-career story may be measuring an incumbent phenomenon that happens to show up first in entry-level statistics.
keyFindings: Entrants are explicitly set aside: 'Job-finding rates for new entrants have declined in recent years, but the drop is modest relative to the declines among job losers and job leavers. Entrants do not appear to be the margin where the action is, and we set them aside in what follows.'

The decline is concentrated by attachment: job-finding rates for strongly attached workers in highly AI-exposed occupations fell roughly 13 percentage points since 2023, against about 2 percentage points for marginally attached workers.

AI exposure is the sorting variable that matters. Within worker types, the post-2023 job-finding deterioration is largest in the most AI-exposed occupations - the exposure gradient is present even after conditioning on attachment.

The unit is job-finding probability, not employment level: this is about how hard it is for an unemployed worker to get re-hired, which is a flow measure and a leading indicator rather than a stock of jobs lost.

Worker types are built from CPS reason-for-unemployment categories - job losers, job leavers, entrants and re-entrants - which is a standard and well-understood decomposition of the unemployment pool.

Implication for the early-career literature: an incumbent-driven hiring freeze in exposed occupations would also depress entry-level hiring, so entrant-focused designs can attribute to entrants an effect that originates with experienced workers.
methodology: CPS-based flow analysis. Monthly job-finding rates are computed from matched Current Population Survey transitions, split by reason-for-unemployment category (job losers, job leavers, entrants, re-entrants) and cross-cut by occupational AI exposure. Trends are compared before and after 2023. This is a descriptive Fed economic brief rather than a working paper: there is no causal identification strategy, no control for the interest-rate cycle, and the AI-exposure grouping does the work of attribution. The strength is the worker-type decomposition, which is rarely applied to the AI question and which most early-career studies do not perform at all.
qualifiers: Tier 1 by publisher, but this is a short descriptive brief, not peer-reviewed research, and the AI attribution rests on an exposure grouping rather than an identified mechanism - the same 2022-2023 macro tightening that OECD blames for the youth gap would also depress job-finding for experienced workers in interest-sensitive professional sectors, and this brief does not rule that out. It enters jobsdata.ai as an overlay because job-finding rate is a different construct from every chart it touches: it is neither a share of jobs displaced nor a share of roles automated, and there is no documented conversion. The 13-versus-2-point contrast should be read as a gradient across worker types rather than a precise pair of estimates. Its main value is as a caution about the level of aggregation in the early-career evidence, and it should be cited alongside the OECD Employment Outlook 2026, which reaches a compatible skeptical conclusion by an entirely different route.
